batch_name: Origins of Greek and Chinese Alchemy; al-Razi as Empiricist
description: Events from F. Sherwood Taylor, The Origins of Greek Alchemy (Ambix, 1937) on the earliest Chinese alchemical record and the Leyden and Stockholm papyri, and from Gerard Heym, Al-Razi and Alchemy (Ambix, 1938) on al-Razi as the founder of experimental alchemy.

texts.title: Leyden and Stockholm Papyri
texts.analysis_html:
The Leyden Papyrus X (Papyrus Graecus Holmiensis) and the Stockholm Papyrus, both now housed in European libraries, are the earliest surviving documentary evidence of the alchemical impulse to make gold-like and silver-like substances in the ancient world. F. Sherwood Taylor, in Ambix (1937), estimates that both were written towards the end of the third century CE, though they are believed to draw on older sources. The Leyden papyrus was edited by O. Lagercrantz (Papyrus Graecus Holmiensis, Uppsala, 1913) and by Berthelot (Archeologie et Histoire des Sciences, Paris, 1906).

Content. Together the papyri contain some hundreds of recipes for the preparation (or, as Taylor notes, sometimes the falsification) of gold, silver, asemos (a white silver-like metal), precious stones, and dyestuffs. The recipes range from crude dilution of genuine gold with copper or cadmia, through surface treatments that produce a convincing appearance of gold on base-metal objects, to more sophisticated alloys. A representative recipe instructs the practitioner to heat copper with iron sulphate, alum, and salt -- a process that evolves sulphuric and hydrochloric acids and removes base metals from the surface of the gold, leaving a thin layer of pure gold for polishing. The Leyden papyrus uses the symbols of Sun and Moon for gold and silver, demonstrating that the planet-metal symbolism characteristic of later Greek alchemy was already in use by the late third century CE.

Significance. Sherwood Taylor is emphatic that the papyri are not in the direct tradition of alchemy: they are nowhere cited by alchemical authors, they lack the spiritual dimension always present in true alchemy, and they make no claim to genuine transmutation. Rather, they are the work of practical craftsmen trying to make gold-like and silver-like alloys, or to falsify genuine precious metals. One papyrus does, however, mention the alchemist Demokritos, indicating that its authors were acquainted with the true alchemical tradition. The papyri thus stand between practical metallurgical craft and the emergence of philosophical alchemy, providing the clearest surviving window into the Egyptian workshop culture that formed one of the two proximate roots of Western alchemy.

events.title: Li Shao-chun Advises Emperor Wu Ti of Han on Alchemical Gold
events.description: The wizard Li Shao-chun advised the Han Emperor Wu Ti (r. 141-87 BCE) that by sacrificing to the kitchen god Tsao, spirits could be summoned, and that cinnabar powder could then be transmuted into yellow gold. Vessels made from this gold, Li Shao-chun claimed, would prolong life. His speech is preserved in the Han Shu (History of the Former Han), chapter XXV, as translated by Arthur Waley: Sacrifice to the stove (tsao) and you will be able to summon things (spirits). Summon spirits and you will be able to change cinnabar powder into yellow gold. With this yellow gold you make vessels to eat and to drink out of. You will then increase your span of life. F. Sherwood Taylor, in Ambix (1937), draws on this passage to conclude that Chinese alchemy was probably in existence at least as early as 200 BCE, antedating the earliest Greek alchemical writings by about two centuries. The central doctrine visible here -- that artificially prepared gold prolongs life because gold is especially rich in the positive Yang principle -- is, Taylor emphasizes, totally absent from Western alchemy of the first millennium CE. The idea that gold could be made from cinnabar (mercury sulphide) reflects the Taoist principle that certain substances rich in Yang can sustain life. This text represents the earliest historically dated alchemical episode in the record: the application of alchemical theory to royal longevity. Although the two great traditions -- Chinese and Hellenistic Egyptian -- developed independently, the Chinese tradition arrived independently at the conception of alchemical gold as a medicine for prolonging life, which would only enter Western alchemy via Arabic intermediaries in the medieval period.
events.scholarly_grounding: F. Sherwood Taylor analyzed the earliest Chinese alchemical records and their relation to Greek alchemy, citing the Han Shu XXV passage translated by Arthur Waley, in The Origins of Greek Alchemy in Ambix vol. 1 no. 1 (1937) pp.30-47.

events.title: Leyden and Stockholm Papyri Compiled in Egypt
events.description: The Leyden Papyrus X (Papyrus Graecus Holmiensis) and the Stockholm Papyrus, both written towards the end of the third century CE in Egypt, are the earliest surviving documentary evidence of the systematic attempt to make gold-like and silver-like substances in the ancient world. F. Sherwood Taylor, in Ambix (1937), describes the papyri as almost wholly practical and devoid of mystical content: together they contain several hundred recipes for the preparation (and in some cases the outright falsification) of gold, silver, asemos (a white silver-like metal), precious stones, and dyestuffs. The recipes range from simple dilution of genuine gold with copper, to surface treatments that produce a thin layer of pure gold on a base-metal object (a predecessor of modern gold plating), to amalgam gilding with mercury. One recipe instructs the practitioner to mix copper with iron sulphate, alum, and salt: heating this combination evolves sulphuric and hydrochloric acids which remove base metals from the surface of the gold, leaving a convincing layer for polishing. The papyri's calligraphy and format suggest they were compiled from older sources. Crucially, while one papyrus makes an incidental mention of the alchemist Demokritos -- establishing a connection to the philosophical alchemical tradition -- the papyri themselves contain no mystical content, no concealed symbolism, and no claim to genuine transmutation. Taylor concludes that they cannot be regarded as the source from which true alchemy developed; they are nowhere cited by alchemical authors. Rather, they represent the practical craft tradition of Egyptian goldsmiths and metalworkers alongside which -- but distinct from which -- the philosophical tradition of Greek alchemy developed. The Leyden papyrus uses the symbols of the Sun and Moon for gold and silver, demonstrating that planet-metal symbolism was already practical in Egypt by ca. 300 CE.
events.scholarly_grounding: F. Sherwood Taylor analyzed the Leyden and Stockholm papyri as the earliest practically-oriented alchemical documents, distinct from the philosophical alchemical tradition, in The Origins of Greek Alchemy in Ambix vol. 1 no. 1 (1937) pp.30-47.

events.title: Al-Razi Transforms Alchemy into an Experimental Science
events.description: Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi (865-925 CE), the Persian physician and natural philosopher known in Latin as Rhazes, composed the Kitab al-Asrar (Book of Secrets) and related alchemical treatises during the height of the Islamic Golden Age, and in doing so became -- in the judgment of Gerard Heym, in Ambix (1938) -- the first to transform theoretical alchemy into a strictly experimental system. Where earlier Greek alchemy (especially the Jabir corpus) had been dominated by Isma'ili speculative philosophical frameworks, al-Razi's alchemical work rejects that speculative philosophy entirely and replaces it with a book of experiments. Al-Razi described specific procedures -- calcination as depriving bodies of their association with one another and burning off any sulphur or oil they contain; sublimation; distillation; crystallization -- and assigned each chemical agent a specific role in transformation. Heym identifies in al-Razi's system the origin of the Mercury-Sal-Sulphur triad of later European alchemy: mercury, ammonium chloride, sulphur, and arsenic (Zarnikh) are treated as four spirits that modify the colour, texture, and transformability of metals, through processes of sublimation, distillation, washing, roasting, and boiling. Al-Razi's theory of matter posited five eternal principles (jauhar): the Creator, soul, matter, time, and space; bodies were composed of indivisible atoms separated by empty space, with the characteristics of the four Aristotelian elements (earth, water, air, fire) determined by atomic density. According to al-Biruni, al-Razi composed 21 alchemical works in total. The Kitab al-Asrar was translated into German by Julius Ruska in 1937. Heym argues that al-Razi's system, though theoretical, is as internally consistent as any other scientific system when judged on its own terms. His influence was acknowledged at Dutch universities as late as the early seventeenth century.
events.scholarly_grounding: Gerard Heym analyzed al-Razi as the creator of experimental alchemy, drawing on Julius Ruska's 1937 German translation of the Kitab Sirr al-Asrar, in Al-Razi and Alchemy in Ambix vol. 1 no. 3 (1938) pp.184-191.
